d.title: Two jobs, and the giveaway is the unit
d.caption: "Is this good?" means something different depending on what *this* is, and the unit of measurement gives it away. Evaluating a **model** asks whether these weights are good, measured on a token or a fixed question. Evaluating an **application** asks whether the system serves users, measured on a RAG answer, an agent trajectory or a guardrail decision. The row that matters most is the ground truth: for an application **nothing but live traffic is ground truth**.

d.title: Four rungs, from free and narrow to expensive and true
d.caption: The ladder's shape is the trade between **applicability and trustworthiness**. Exact metrics are deterministic and free and apply only where correctness is checkable. Reference-based metrics are cheap and automatic, and 8.3 measures them scoring an **inverted sentence at ROUGE-1 of exactly 1.0000**. Model-graded scales to any task and is noisy in ways you have to measure. Human judgement is the only real ground truth, at a cost that bounds how much of it you can have.

d.title: Four terms, and the one that decides how large your eval set can be
d.caption: Offline against online is a question of *when*; reference-based against reference-free is a question of **what bounds you**. A gold answer per case means somebody has to write it, so annotation effort caps the set size — and that is why reference-free metrics matter structurally rather than conveniently: faithfulness, answer relevancy and context precision all need **no gold answer**, so the set can be as large as your traffic.

d.title: Perplexity is the pretraining loss with an exponential on the front
d.caption: 7.2's loss, exponentiated. `H` is the mean negative log-probability per token — in nats for natural log — and perplexity is e^H. The reading that makes it intuitive: **the model is choosing among about 165 equally-likely options per token** on this text. Which also means a perplexity of 165 is not a quality statement on its own; it is a statement about this model's uncertainty on this particular text, with this particular tokenizer.

d.title: Same model, same text, same surprise — perplexity from 86 to 184
d.caption: The denominator is a **token count**, and token count is a property of the tokenizer rather than of the text. Holding the model's total surprise fixed at 245.0513 nats and only changing how the text is split, perplexity reads anywhere from **86.0973 to 183.8017 — a 2.13× range from tokenisation alone**. Nothing about the model or the text changed. Which is why cross-tokenizer perplexity comparisons are meaningless and bits-per-byte exists.

d.title: Four valid uses and three invalid ones
d.caption: Perplexity is sound wherever **both confounds are held fixed** — same tokenizer, same held-out set — which is exactly comparing checkpoints of one run. It is invalid across tokenizers, measured above at a 2.13× range; invalid across corpora, because it is a model-and-corpus property; and invalid on a chat model, because **low perplexity is not helpfulness, safety or correctness**. Where you need a cross-tokenizer comparison, use bits-per-byte: the denominator is bytes, which nothing can game.

d.title: Eight metrics, and what each one is blind to
d.caption: Read the gotcha column as the real content. **BLEU is n-gram precision and ROUGE is recall**, so neither sees meaning: ROUGE rewards overlap rather than faithfulness, which is why a summary that reverses a claim can score perfectly. BERTScore is semantic and therefore **model-dependent**, so it inherits whatever its embedding model is bad at. Only the last row is checkable rather than correlated, and it needs executable tests.
cells: better recall of meaning than BLEU

d.title: pass@k, and the boundary that makes it read 1.0000
d.caption: The estimator answers: from n samples of which c were correct, what is the chance a draw of k contains at least one correct? It is exact, which puts it on the bottom rung of 8.1's ladder where it belongs. The trap is in the boundary: **at n=10 and c=1, pass@10 is 1.0000** — because drawing 10 of 10 samples must include the one that passed. The last row shows the fix: with n=100 and c=5, pass@10 is 0.4162 and genuinely informative. **n must substantially exceed k.**

d.title: Where overlap metrics are still exactly right
d.caption: The failure measured above is about **open-ended** output, where many phrasings are correct and overlap says nothing about which. For translation and summarisation **regression** — same inputs, same references, version N against N+1 — the metric is used as a *relative* signal on a fixed comparison, and that is what it is good at. The sin is reading an absolute ROUGE score as a quality claim; the legitimate use is reading a change in it as a regression alarm.

nodes.label: That is a regression alarm

d.title: Ten benchmarks, read by their format column
d.caption: The format decides how gameable a number is. **Multiple-choice can be answered by elimination and by memorisation**, and seven of these ten are multiple-choice or mixed. The three that are execution-scored — HumanEval/MBPP on unit tests, SWE-bench on whether a patch passes — resist most forms of gaming, because a memorised answer still has to run. And the two judge-scored rows inherit every bias from 8.6.

d.title: Memorisation and competence produce the same number
d.caption: The mechanism is unglamorous: these datasets are **public**, discussed in papers, reproduced in blog posts and GitHub repositories — and pretraining corpora are scraped from the web. So a model can have seen the test, and **nothing in the score distinguishes having learned the skill from having learned the answers**. Which makes a benchmark number an *upper bound* on capability rather than an estimate of it, and makes a suspiciously high score on an old benchmark the signature to look for.

nodes.label: The model may have seen the test
So a score is an upper bound
And a fresh held-out set is the check

d.title: A benchmark number without its harness is not reproducible
d.caption: Scores shift with formatting, few-shot count and answer-parsing — and that is not a minor caveat, it means **the number is a property of the harness as much as of the model.** Two papers reporting MMLU for the same model can legitimately differ by several points without either being wrong. Which is why the instruction is always to report the harness and its settings, and why `lm-evaluation-harness` exists at all: it is a fixed harness so the remaining difference is the model.

nodes.label: So report the harness and settings
Which is why a fixed harness exists

d.title: The update rule, and why a win against a weaker model is worth so little
d.caption: Elo's expected score is a logistic in the rating gap, and the update is K times the surprise. Read the right-hand column: beating an **equal** opponent moves you 16.00 points, and beating one you were already **400 Elo above** moves you 2.91 — because you were expected to win 90.91% of the time and did. Which is the self-correcting property that makes the scale stable, and also why a new model needs many games against *comparable* opponents to find its level.

d.title: A 20-Elo gap needs about 1,163 comparisons
d.caption: 20 Elo sounds meaningful and corresponds to winning **52.88%** of comparisons — which is close enough to a coin flip that distinguishing it takes real sample size. At 100 comparisons the 95% interval is **±68.2 Elo**, so the whole leaderboard's middle is inside one interval. At 1,000 it is ±21.6, which is just about enough. **Resolving a 20-Elo gap needs about 1,163 comparisons**, and that is per pair of models.

d.title: Pairwise is more reliable, and that is not a preference
d.caption: Pointwise scoring gives an absolute number, which is convenient and **requires the judge to hold a stable internal scale across every case** — the same thing 7.4 showed humans cannot do. Pairwise asks only which of two is better, which is the comparison judges are actually reliable at, and it is what powers MT-Bench and Arena-Hard. The cost is that you get a ranking rather than a level, so you cannot say *how* good without an anchor.

nodes.label: Cost: a ranking, not a level

d.title: Four biases, each with a mechanical mitigation
d.caption: None of these is a reason not to use a judge; each has a fix that costs a second call or a preprocessing step. **Position bias is the one that is free to fix and most often skipped** — run both orders and either average or require agreement, and an uncontrolled judge is measuring position plus quality with no way to separate them. Self-preference is the one that needs a *different* judge family rather than a better prompt.
